source: Tsui (2026, v3 of 2507.02778) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot
finding: Same error injected as user-written (external) or model-written (internal); only the chat role header differs. Models fix the external one and miss the internal one. The updated version tests closed models and the model's own natural errors.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: 64.5% average blind spot. Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-maths (BIG-Bench Mistake logic and object tracking): 62.8%. On the model's own natural errors, only 4.3% to 10.8% were caught once the same error was shown as external.
limits: Only the role header differs; role and turn position cannot be varied separately. Closed models need prefill, which most APIs lack.
agent_relevance: Role reframe works on injected errors, but on natural errors it rescues only 4% to 11%. Treat reframe as a small gain, not a fix.
quote: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones

source: Tsui (2026, v3) Section 4.4 and Table 3: reasoning models and appended Wait
finding: Reasoning models show a small, even negative, blind spot. Appending Wait to a non-reasoning model nearly closes the gap to its reasoning sibling.
limits: Injected-error benchmark, not natural errors. Qwen3 non-thinking mode still shows the blind spot.
agent_relevance: For a current reasoning model the role-reframe gap (gap 4) is mostly closed by training. Reframing helps non-reasoning or non-thinking modes. A Wait cue is the cheap equivalent.
quote: Reasoning models exhibit a small, even negative, Self-Correction Blind Spot

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: Models can tell their own text from others. Self-preference grows with self-recognition, and fine-tuning the recognition ability moves the preference with it.
numbers: GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate at telling itself from another source out of the box (summarisation). Self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition ability.
limits: Summarisation, 2024 models. Not maths. Correlation plus fine-tune control, not proof for reasoning steps.
agent_relevance: A role reframe (call the step someone else's) may be seen through if the model recognises its own style. An independent second sample is a stronger lever than disguising authorship.
quote: GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate distinguishing itself

source: Xu et al. (2024) Pride and Prejudice: LLM amplifies self-bias in self-refinement
finding: Six LLMs favour their own output when judging it. Self-refine raises this bias over iterations. Larger models and accurate external feedback reduce it.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini, LLaMA2, Mixtral, DeepSeek on translation, constrained generation and maths (100 examples from the MATH test set). Bias present in all models and tasks.
limits: Maths part is small (100 items). 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Self-judged progress is inflated. S6 progress markers should not be the model's own claim alone; use an external check or a different sample.
quote: self-bias is prevalent in all examined LLMs

source: He et al. (2025) DeltaBench: can LLMs detect errors in long chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Long CoTs from QwQ, DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking are annotated section by section. Error detection by critics and PRMs is poor. o1-style models are not better critics. About a quarter of sections are redundant.
numbers: Best critic GPT-4-turbo-128k F1 40.76 overall. GPT-4o-mini 37.82. GPT-4o 30.49. DeepSeek-R1 24.73. o1-preview 19.89. Best PRM Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B 29.22. On average 27% of sections redundant. R1 self-critique is 36% lower than its critique of other o1-like models.
limits: Macro F1 per sample, section-level labels, early-2025 critics. Math, code, PCB and general mixed.
agent_relevance: Locating errors inside a long reasoning trace without ground truth is about 30 to 40 F1 at best, so a step-level monitor in S6 will be noisy. The 27% redundant sections are a target for stop rules. Self-critique is worse than cross-critique.
quote: existing PRMs cannot identify the errors in long CoTs effectively

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: identifying process errors in mathematical reasoning
finding: Earliest-error step identification on maths solutions. Prompted critic models beat open PRMs. F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples.
numbers: Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5, GPT-4o-0806 61.9. Open-source critics use majority vote over 8 samples; GPT-4o greedy; o1-mini single sample. Open PRMs in the 26 to 58 band on the headline chart.
limits: Per-subset table text was garbled so only chart averages are recorded. Models are late 2024. Harder from GSM8K to OlympiadBench.
agent_relevance: Cost-quality anchor for gap 5: a reasoning-model critic reaches high F1 on ProcessBench, but DeltaBench (d05) shows long-CoT traces are much harder.
quote: QwQ-32B-Preview, has demonstrated the critique capability competitive with the proprietary model GPT-4o

source: Khalifa et al. (2025) Process reward models that think (ThinkPRM)
finding: A long-CoT verifier trained on 1K chains (8K process labels) beats the same base model used as a plain LLM judge, and beats discriminative PRMs, on ProcessBench. The plain judge often returns invalid output.
numbers: F1 on OlympiadBench / OmniMath subsets of ProcessBench: R1-Qwen-14B as judge 72.8 / 67.8 (13.3% / 18.6% bad outputs); ThinkPRM 87.3 / 85.7 (2.3% / 2.3%). R1-Qwen-1.5B judge 5.0 / 5.4 (51% / 55% invalid) vs ThinkPRM 76.3 / 75.7. At equal token budget ThinkPRM beats the judge by 7.2 F1 on a ProcessBench subset.
limits: Needs a fine-tuned verifier with some process labels, so not a zero-training monitor. Subsets of ProcessBench only.
agent_relevance: A reasoning-model verifier that writes a step-by-step check is the best label-free monitor of the three options; plain judge prompts are unreliable (invalid outputs up to 55%).
quote: LLM-as-a-judge with reasoning models suffer from issues that limits their utility as generative verifiers

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Self-verification limitations on reasoning and planning
finding: GPT-4 self-critique lowers accuracy. A sound external verifier raises it. Merely re-prompting with a sound verifier keeps most of the gain, so the critique text itself matters little.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM critiques LLM 3%, LLM + sound verifier 36% to 38%, sampling k=15 28%, k=25 42%, self-consistency 6%. Graph colouring 16% to 2% with self-critique. Blocksworld 40% to 55% with self-critique (a rise).
limits: GPT-4 (2023), toy puzzle and planning domains. Blocksworld self-critique rose, so the drop is not universal.
agent_relevance: Supports gating revisions on a tool check (gap 5). In Game of 24, sampling with a sound check (42% at k=25) beat self-critique by a wide margin.
quote: significant performance collapse with self-critique and significant performance gains with sound external verification

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey up to May 2024. Self-correction from prompted LLMs alone does not show success on general tasks; it works where reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning can help.
numbers: Qualitative survey. Abstract and introduction read. Three headline conclusions as stated in the abstract.
limits: Survey stops at May 2024. Only abstract and intro read, not the case tables.
agent_relevance: Independent survey-level confirmation of K03 and K05, but pre-reasoning-model.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning models better express their confidence
finding: Six reasoning models express verbalised confidence better than their non-reasoning twins in 33 of 36 settings. Calibration improves as the chain unfolds, which does not happen for non-reasoning models. Slow-thinking behaviours drive it.
numbers: 33 of 36 settings strictly better. GLM-Z1 vs GLM-4 on NonambigQA: 0.07 lower accuracy, yet ECE 0.037 lower and AUROC 0.078 higher. Reasoning-model Brier score falls along the chain; non-reasoning Brier is lowest at zero CoT.
limits: Open models up to 32B (Qwen3, R1-Distill, QwQ, GLM-Z1, EXAONE-Deep, OR1). Mostly knowledge QA plus SuperGPQA and MMLU-Pro maths subsets. No test of confidence as a stop or switch trigger. Not frontier closed models.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 10: late-in-chain verbalised confidence is usable as a signal. No evidence yet that it works as a stop or switch trigger. Read it late, not at the start.
quote: reasoning models become increasingly better calibrated as their CoT unfolds

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Token-probability confidence over sliding groups of 2,048 tokens. A trace whose lowest group confidence falls under a threshold is stopped mid-generation and low-confidence traces are dropped from the vote. This is a live abandon trigger measured against a majority-vote budget.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B AIME 2025: pass@1 91.8, majority vote at 512 samples 97.0, DeepConf@512 99.9, tokens cut by up to 84.7%. Online variants vs majority at K=512 on AIME24, AIME25, BRUMO25, HMMT25: DeepConf-low saves 43% to 79% tokens (mean 62.88% on DeepSeek-8B), with a few accuracy drops (Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 minus 0.9). DeepConf-high saves 18% to 59%.
limits: Needs token log-probabilities, which many closed APIs hide. Authors list confident-but-wrong traces as a key limit. Baseline is majority vote, not a single chain with no trigger.
agent_relevance: Strongest current evidence that an abandon rule on a confidence signal saves tokens without losing accuracy (partial answer to gap 1, and to gap 10 for open-weight models). Not a hand-written repeated-step rule.
quote: exhibit high confidence on incorrect reasoning paths

source: Fu et al. (2025) Efficiently scaling LLM reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Probe-In-The-Middle: at a fixed interval (for example every 64 tokens) a probe asks the model for its current answer, then the probe is discarded. If probed answers stay the same, the answer is treated as settled and generation stops. Answer stabilisation occurs whether or not the answer is right.
numbers: Up to 50% compute saving and 3.3x higher throughput in serving, with no accuracy drop. On the MATH workload only about 10% of tokens were saved. DeepSeek-R1 uses about 3x more tokens than needed.
limits: A fixed-interval check is used as an early-exit rule and is not compared with a stall-triggered check. Stable but wrong answers are not caught.
agent_relevance: A fixed-interval progress check is cheap and works for stopping (partial answer to gap 2). No head-to-head with a stall trigger yet.
quote: intermediate answers frequently stabilize

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At each action transition word (Wait, Alternatively) the model is forced to give a trial answer and its confidence is checked. If confidence passes a threshold, thinking stops. About 75% of samples contain an early point where exit gives a correct answer.
numbers: 11 reasoning models, 10 benchmarks: chain length cut by 19.1% to 80.1%, accuracy +0.3 to +5.0 points. R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: AIME24 41.7 to 49.2 with tokens 13,765 to 9,839; MATH-500 87.4 to 89.8 with 3,858 to 2,143 tokens. 36.7% of samples needed under half the original chain. Threshold 0.95; too low a threshold overcorrects.
limits: Open models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 families). Compression is larger on easy sets, accuracy gain larger on hard sets.
agent_relevance: A transition-point trigger keyed to Wait beats the vanilla chain on accuracy and tokens at once, including AIME24. Closest direct evidence for gap 1 and 2, on 2025 open models. It is a stop rule, not a switch rule.
quote: about 75% samples contain such pearls

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer convergence as a signal for early stopping in reasoning
finding: Models reach their final answer after about 60% of reasoning steps on maths. Stop when the probed answer has stayed the same for several steps.
numbers: Convergence after about 60% of steps. Answer-consistency early stop cuts tokens by over 40% on NaturalQuestions while raising accuracy. Five benchmarks, five open-weight models.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; per-benchmark maths numbers not read. Open models.
agent_relevance: Second source for stable-answer stopping. Same limit as d12: a stable wrong answer passes.
quote: models typically converge to their final answers after 60% of the reasoning steps

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does thinking more always help? Mirage of test-time scaling
finding: Appending Wait to extend thinking raises accuracy first, then lowers it. The authors argue the gain is extra output variance. Parallel thinking at the same token budget with majority vote does better.
numbers: GSM8K R1-Distill: accuracy 82.2% to 87.3% as tokens rise, then falls to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: Wait out to 16,000 tokens gives minus 11.8%; the same tokens as parallel samples give plus 10.1%. At a 16K budget parallel beats Wait by about 22% and exact-budget forcing by about 47%.
limits: Small distilled R1 models, 32K cap, NeurIPS 2025. Answer selection uses the model's own likelihood. Not frontier models.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8 for small open reasoning models: parallel plus vote beats sequential Wait at equal tokens. The clash with s1 is a setting difference (s1 curves flatten rather than fall).
quote: consistent pattern of initial performance improvements from additional thinking followed by a decline

source: Hassid et al. (2025/2026) Don't overthink it: preferring shorter thinking chains
finding: Among samples for one question the shorter chains are more often right. short-m@k runs k chains in parallel, stops when the first m finish, and votes. It beats majority vote at the same or lower compute.
numbers: Shortest vs longest chain: up to 34.5% accuracy gap. short-1@k matches or beats majority@k at low compute with up to 40% fewer tokens. short-3@k beats majority@k at all budgets: QwQ-32B at 80k tokens per question +2%, R1-670B at 100k +4%. Up to 33% wall-time cut. Four open reasoning models, temperature 0.7, 32,768 cap.
limits: Open reasoning models (LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B), maths benchmarks. Majority vote overtakes short-1@k at large budgets.
agent_relevance: Two rules at equal tokens: stop a chain early and prefer short chains. Supports a length-based abandon trigger and parallel sampling over longer chains (gap 8).
quote: longer thinking does not necessarily translate to improved performance

source: SETS (Google, 2025) Self-enhanced test-time scaling: self-verification and self-correction
finding: One model samples, verifies each sample, and corrects it. This is compared at equal compute with majority-vote repeated sampling. The gain depends on how well the model verifies itself.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Flash-Lite thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Qwen3-235B. Gains largest where self-verification F1 is high (trip planning, Gemini 1.5 Pro verification F1 95.74). Weak self-verification (Claude 3.5 Sonnet on LiveBench reasoning) gave little gain. Majority-vote repeated sampling saturates.
limits: Table values for the AIME and MATH rows were garbled in text extraction, so no per-benchmark maths number is recorded.
agent_relevance: A counter-example to the no-self-correction rule when the model verifies reliably. The gate 'correct only what you verified' is the right design. Not a clean maths-only comparison.
quote: when the models' self-verification and self-correction performance is weak

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking (v3, Nov 2025): three regimes
finding: In controllable puzzles the thinking trace behaves differently by difficulty. Easy: the right answer appears early, then the model keeps exploring wrong ones. Medium: wrong first, right later. Hard: it fixates on an early wrong answer and never recovers.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi: accuracy along the thinking trace falls with position for N=1 to 4, rises for N=5 to 7, and is near zero for N 8 and above. Models include Claude 3.7 Thinking, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini.
limits: Puzzle environments, not competition maths. Part of the collapse is a token-limit or unsolvable-instance artifact (see K19).
agent_relevance: Direct support for a difficulty-gated rule (gap 3): stop after the first verified answer on easy items, force a switch on fixation for hard ones. The gate itself is not tested.
quote: for simpler problems, reasoning models often find the correct solution early in their thinking but then continue exploring incorrect solutions

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: reasoning models can learn when to think
finding: Skipping thinking (NoThinking) matches full thinking on easy MATH levels 1 to 3 at far fewer tokens. RL teaches the model to pick the mode by difficulty.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: response length cut 50.9%, 63.5%, 44.7% on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME2024 with accuracy +4.1, +1.4, +1.6. Averaged over three maths sets length cut 53% and accuracy +2.4. Thinking keeps a clear benefit on hard problems.
limits: 1.5B and 7B distilled models; mode choice is learned by RL, not a prompt rule. Not a test of a hand-written gate on a frontier model.
agent_relevance: A difficulty gate has value (gap 3) but this gate was trained. A hand-written gate on item difficulty is untested.
quote: is a better choice for relatively simple tasks

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: stall rule and ablations
finding: Reflexion's hand-written stall rule: reflect when the same action and response repeat for more than 3 cycles or more than 30 actions are taken. Ablations show the written reflection adds to plain episodic memory.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct-only plateaus at 22% hallucination with no recovery; with reflection 130 of 134 tasks in 12 trials. HotPotQA with ground-truth context: self-reflection adds 8 absolute points over episodic memory of the last trajectory. HumanEval Rust, 50 hard problems: no unit tests 52%, other rows 60% and 68%.
limits: Not maths. A repeat-in-environment stall is not a stall in a reasoning chain. HotPotQA and code, GPT-4 era. No equal-token control.
agent_relevance: Partial evidence for gap 9 (a written lesson beats raw memory) outside maths, and the stall rule used in practice. The maths test has not been run.
quote: if the agent executes the same action and receives the same response for more than 3 cycles

source: Dignath and Buettner (2008) Components of fostering self-regulated learning: meta-analysis, primary and secondary school
finding: Two meta-analyses of self-regulated learning interventions. Training raises academic performance, strategy use and motivation. Maths interventions have higher effects than reading or writing.
numbers: 49 primary and 35 secondary studies, 357 effect sizes in total. Average effect size 0.69. Higher effects in mathematics than in reading/writing or other subjects, and higher when researchers rather than regular teachers delivered the training.
limits: Only the abstract page was readable (paywall). The maths-specific effect size and the metacognition-only sub-effect were not found. Researcher-delivered effects overstate what teachers get.
agent_relevance: Sets the human prior for gap 7: training works, with an average d about 0.7 and more so in maths. The size for metacognition-only training is still unrecorded.
quote: interventions attained higher effects when conducted in the scope of mathematics

source: Wang et al. (2025) Wait, we don't need to Wait: removing thinking tokens improves reasoning efficiency (NoWait)
finding: Suppressing reflection tokens (Wait, Hmm) at inference shortens chains by 27% to 51% across five R1-style families and ten benchmarks without losing accuracy.
numbers: Chain length cut 27% to 51% on text, image and video reasoning; QwQ-32B and others on AIME 2024 and 2025.
limits: Abstract, introduction and figure text read; the per-benchmark accuracy table was not read in detail. Open R1-style models.
agent_relevance: Evidence against forced rechecking (gap 8): removing the reflection cue costs little, so Wait-style extension does not clearly earn its tokens on these models. Contrasts with s1, where forcing helped slightly.
quote: explicit self-reflection, signaled by tokens such as
